1. VSCode / Cursor

You have no excuse not to use a modern IDE.
Unless you’re an “old-head,” VIM/EMACS are strictly worse for your velocity.
Stop using Jupyter Notebooks for everything.

If you use them for source code, you are doing things wrong.

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
2. Project Structure


Modularity

Separate source code from sweeps.

Make your source code a python module

Separate scripts from plotting.
Notebooks are for plots, not logic.
Example: bert_adapter.py


Version Control

Git early, git often.
Collaborating? Use Pull Requests.
Working alone? Use Branches.
Example: README.md (Git Flow Intro)

3. UV: The New Standard
UV is a major innovation over pip and conda.

Speed: Orders of magnitude faster than pip.
Reproducibility:

pyproject.toml tracks everything.
uv.lock ensures the exact environment every time.

Example: pyproject.toml

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
UV vs. Conda


The Problems

Local vs. Cluster: “I developed code locally, but the VACC environment is throwing version errors.”
Collaboration: “A coworker cloned my repo, but it won’t run due to their global NumPy version.”


The Solutions

Local Environments: Envs live inside your project folder.
Reproducibility: The lockfile ensures byte-for-byte matching.
Deep Performance: Global cache using hard-linking.
Example: pyproject.toml

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Pydantic: Strong Typing


The Problems

Boilerplate: Constant manual parsing and validation of dictionaries.
Silent Bugs: Passing \(N \times M\) when \(M \times N\) was expected.
Interface Bloat: Parameters passed through 5+ nested layers.


The Solutions

Pydantic Validation: Catch errors at the boundary.
LLM Context: Gives LLMs the precise “slots” needed.
Baked-in Logic: Logic belongs in the data definition.
Example: schema.py

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Snakemake

Problem 1: Advisor wants you to regenerate a figure from 6 months ago—what was the script? What were the parameters?
Problem 2: You changed src/core/utils.py and now you need to know which of your 500 simulation results are now invalid.
The Solution: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).
Automation: One command (snakemake) to run everything in the correct order.
Reproducibility: The Snakefile is the documentation.

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Snakemake: Workflow Orchestration


The Problems

Amnesia: “I changed code; what results are now invalid?”
Lost parameters: “How did I generate this figure 6 months ago?”
Batch Hell: VACC repo littered with 10M Slurm batch files.


The Solutions

DAG Generation: Snakemake knows exactly what needs to run.
Self-Documentation: The Snakefile is the record.
Registry: High-level rules replace manual Slurm scripts.
Example: Snakefile

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Defensive Coding: Testing

Unit Testing: Whenever you write a significant function, define what “correct” looks like.

Shape Checks: Is the matrix the size I expect?
Analytical Baseline: Does my numerical model match a known analytical solution?
Regression: Does my “Optimized” algorithm give the same answer as my “Naive/Slow” one?

Integration Testing: Ensuring the “plumbing” works end-to-end.

The 1-Epoch Test: Does the pipeline run on a tiny dataset without crashing?
The Smoke Test: If I run for one epoch, does the loss decrease even a tiny bit?

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Testing


The Problems

Silent Regression: “I only changed the colors; why are my results different?”
Legacy Terror: “My code changed so much I can’t run old figures.”
Vibe Blindness: Trusting LLM code without verification.


The Solutions

Unit Tests: Shape checks & Analytical baselines.
Integration Tests: “The 1-Epoch Test” for pipeline sanity.
Vibe Coding: Use tests to verify LLM-generated logic.
CI/CD: Auto-run tests on every push to GitHub.
Example: test_nlp_logic.py
